title: Seneca at his worst
hookLine: from exile he flatters the emperor Claudius in a consolation, hoping for recall (Consolation to Polybius)

lines: A MESSAGE YOU'D RATHER NOT SEE.
cards: Somewhere there's a message you'd rather not see again. A post praising a boss who held your job in their hands. A toast that said more than you meant.
Flattering someone powerful out of fear is an old habit. Seneca had it too, in writing, and the writing survived. In the year 41 he was sent into exile on the island of Corsica.
From there he wrote a letter of comfort to a grieving man who happened to sit very close to the emperor.

teach.b: First, the exile. Early in the reign of the emperor Claudius, Seneca was charged with adultery with Julia Livilla, the emperor's niece, and banished to Corsica.
The ancient sources don't let us say whether the charge was true; Cassius Dio says the empress Messalina was behind the charges against Julia.
Either way, he was cut off from Rome, his career and his friends, with no end date. Second, the letter.

teach.h: PRAISE FOR CLAUDIUS, SENT VIA POLYBIUS.
teach.b: Polybius, a freed slave who had become a powerful secretary to Claudius, had lost his brother. Seneca wrote him a consolation. Parts of it sound like Seneca anywhere: grief, time, the shortness of life.
But again and again he turns to the emperor. Look to Caesar for comfort, he tells Polybius, and he praises Claudius's mercy in words so lavish they're hard to read now.
In passing he hopes that mercy might one day reach Corsica too. Third, what came after.
It didn't work. Seneca stayed in exile eight years, until Agrippina had him recalled to tutor her son Nero. When Claudius died, a savage satire mocked him, and Cassius Dio names Seneca as its author.
Dio, writing long afterward, also says Seneca later tried to suppress a flattering book he'd sent from exile, out of shame. Fourth, why the path reads this.
It's the same pen that wrote about fearing nothing and holding every hour.
Ideas don't turn into character just because you can write them beautifully.
Under enough fear, even Seneca bent. In a way he told us so himself: not wise, only trying to be less bad each day.

how: Some readers of Seneca read the Consolation to Polybius alongside his finest letters, as a reminder that the teacher fell short of his own teaching under pressure.

o: a public speech of praise for the dead
flattery of the powerful, offered out of fear
the step from boyhood into Roman adulthood

games.q: Seneca at his worst — tap the pairs.
p: had Seneca recalled to tutor Nero
says Seneca later tried to suppress it

s: the flattering letter got Seneca recalled within a year
he stayed on Corsica eight years, until Agrippina brought him back.
Polybius was a freed slave who became a powerful imperial secretary
that's why a letter to him could reach the emperor.
we know for certain whether the adultery charge against Seneca was true
the sources don't settle it; Cassius Dio blames the empress Messalina.

games.q: you're Seneca on Corsica, years from home. the emperor's powerful secretary has lost his brother. what do you write?
o: a plain, honest letter of comfort.
comfort, laced with lavish praise of the emperor and a hint about your exile.
games.why: he praised Claudius lavishly and hoped for mercy. it didn't bring him home, and a later historian says he grew ashamed of it.

practice: If a memory comes, let it be one time you flattered someone because you feared them or needed something from them: a boss, a landlord, someone with a say over your life.
Don't punish yourself; just look at the fear underneath, without judging it. Seneca on Corsica knew some version of it too.

wordCard.voice: Adulatio. Latin for flattery, fawning: from exile, Seneca flattered the emperor in a letter of comfort, hoping to be called home. It didn't work, and he seems to have regretted it. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: flattery, fawning. The thing Seneca warns against in other works, and does here.

carryVoice: Your line: even seneca. Knowing the good and doing it under pressure are two different skills. Day five hundred fifteen, done.
